en: Was I destined to miss death in the field,
Was this the day death would come?
If Death summons, it casts its spell, it seems;
Upon the mighty bowman
It lays its cold hand, it seems.
We walk among the living,
Created as mortal servants;
When the poor soul closes its eyes,
It is shut in the grave it sees but once—
Such is harsh, true falsehood.
From the stony ravine where battle rages,
From the barren gorge where no bird flies,
A shudder came and consciousness fled.
From the thick-ranked rocky gorge,
Fighting in this way,
Across the broad open field,
Sweetly arrayed for display,
Among a singular people who race their horses,
He was a lion born to fight.
In the deep valley of Keng-Kol,
Along the great Talas,
Sarybai was a hero—
Is it fitting to fear a child?
Could a ravenous lion be fainthearted,
Could he be a fool like me?
The Kyrgyz are those I shall fight,
The great prince Semetey.
I shall destroy the Argyn camp,
I shall destroy the Nogai stronghold,
I shall lay waste the Kyrgyz marches.
Leaving not a scrap of this people—
Could a witless coward who fears a child
Be a hero like me?
The fate ordained by the Creator
I have witnessed many times before.
Finding no mountain to strike,
Finding no enemy to fight,
Finding no stone to grind my teeth upon,
Finding no head to sever,
Driven wild by restless ardor,
Like a wolf straining at its tether,
Stirred up by the very wind—
It seems I came to suffer grievous pain
At the hands of this boy.
It seems I came to die
At the hands of lion-hearted Seytek.
Our dream has turned awry;
Our cause has been undone.
Ah, Seytek is a true hero,
His fortune is complete;
He has eighty-four weapons,
And their sweep is fire.
He is a fierce one born of the Kyrgyz;
Never has his like existed in an age.
Seytek became an ember in my heart.
My name is brave Sarybai,
The courser beneath me is my wings;
To make the whole world tremble
Has ever been my custom.
My host beyond counting is assembled;
I applied all my heroic skill,
But found no way at all.
He is a boy beyond reckoning;
I shall drive a spear into his breast.
I shall thrust the spear with force,
Smash him into fragments,
And hurl him aside in pieces.
I shall slaughter his village and take the spoils;
If the day does not end, I shall return.
An omen is evil, a dream is evil,
When fortune turns against you, the deed is evil,
And evil is the coat you lift to wear.”
Not a foal remained among the shod horses;
The uproar had wholly vanished.
I, Sarybai, bearing the name of khan—
Evil is the force that abandoned me.
Evil is the force of an outsider’s son,
Evil is strife that comes from within,
Evil is fire that rises from the core.
Chañdayak, who deserted me—
Evil is the dog who knew my secrets.
If true death comes, let me die;
Let me see what courage there is
In that sniveling boy.
Kulansur, who yields to no pursuit,
Is a creature born one of a kind,
Like a host of encircling wolves,
A beast come plainly into view.
Upon Kulansur, who yields to no pursuit,
I shall cast a cold lasso;
Kulansur, who will not yield when asked,
I shall escort away through spilled blood.
I shall raise an unflagging tumult,
Stir boundless calamity and uproar,
Find my chance and wreak slaughter,
And avenge my ancient grudge.
I shall defeat the princely people;
If the sly boy falls into my hands,
I shall drink his blood like kumis.
I shall open everyone’s eyes;
If by chance he falls into my hands,
I shall feast upon his young liver,
Spear his mighty warriors,
And conquer his hardy men.
If he falls into my hands, he will go no farther—
So saying, Sarybai
Gathered as much courage as he could,
Venom touching his blackened mouth;
He took heart and thundered,
And the mortal frame
Of humankind shuddered from head to foot.
When he raged, calamity arose,
And wherever he struck was leveled.
Wrath burst from his courage,
Venom poured toward all he faced—
Thus Sarybai advanced.
From the depths of hell itself,
Born as the Antichrist,
Sarybai had come.
Mustering all his courage,
His glaring eyes became fire,
His insides blazed like embers;
His bristling hair stood wild,
His inner nature was transformed,
Revealing blood-drinking ferocity.
When he cried out in rage,
He seemed about to swallow the whole world;
Anyone who witnessed his full fury
Fled in panic, crying, “I am dead!”
Had he fought for six years,
Had he slain the armies of the world,
Had he endured grievous hardship,
His strength spent and his head aching—
Such was the fearsome boar’s
Demeanor when you saw him.
Onto the broad field of death,
He came forth and faced the fray,
Bearing twelve different weapons—
May they be accursed.
Let me learn whether he is a man:
Rejoicing at the thought of death,
He prepared to unleash his wrath,
Wrapped himself in battle gear,
His ferocity plain to see,
And donned his armored coat.
His manly courage showed
As he put on his precious mail,
Starting as though seized by frenzy,
And saddled Tookyzyl.
He girded on the black-steel, blood-shedding
Zulfiqar sword.
Fleeing before the sight of his wrath,
The smoothly flowing river,
The plane tree and fruit-bearing willow—
Before his courage and fury,
Even speechless beasts submitted.
Sarybai, son of a monster,
Armed himself and rode to war.
The ill-fated boar
Found the strife he had sought.
When the seventh day came,
The appointed, promised day,
And its time was fully reached,
When dawn shone clear,
And light fell upon the earth,
Brave Seytek’s seer,
Who knew the face of the world,
Went out to the watch and saw him;
Such a thing happened in the world.
At that very watchpost,
At the dark eye of the spring,
Beside the great plane tree,
When your khan-father Manas lived,
Scouts stood nearby.
At that same watchpost,
After ranging through many lands,
Scouts who knew every country
And guards who bent beneath their vigilance stood.
Brave Seytek, the prince’s son,
Seytek, whose four kinds of livestock stood ready,
Kept eighty sentries and five scouts
Patrolling the land.
To spy an enemy from afar,
They struck the great drum with a crash,
As though ready to devour any raven they saw;
If even a crow appeared from afar,
They would carry word to the city.
They stood throughout the land,
To learn the truth
About kinsman and enemy,
Serving as messengers between them.
What the hollows were like, what the mountains were like—
They were guides who returned at a run.
At the slightest stirring they turned back;
At the command to speak, they instantly
Reported whatever they saw
To lion-maned Seytek,
Traveling under concealment,
And whenever anything occurred,
Bringing word of what appeared.
The diviner at the watchpost,
An inheritance from the forefathers,
A keen eye handed down by heroes,
Spoke his words clearly
And lived openly among men.
When Sarybai, son of a monster,
Rode out for single combat,
The brave diviner saw him,
And at once brought the lion-maned hero
News for Seytek.
Then the diviner
Spoke these words:
“Lion-maned Seytek, hear me;
I have seen a marvel such as this.
In all the world I have never seen
A man of such surpassing terror.
Do not refuse what I say:
To the ravaging monster,
Hero, you granted a term of seven days;
The enraged Sarybai
Is a fearsome calamity such as this.
His lion eyes are blazing,
His overflowing rage is boiling;
He is swollen like a blue tick—
Such is his appearance.
Armed and furious,
Draped in black velvet,
Khan Sarybai rages;
His stare is like a tiger’s.
No man could face
That foul-natured boar;
His roar is like a lion’s.
The ravager who drives the people mad
Seems able to grind them into sand beneath his feet.
No living soul can withstand his wrestling;
Those he meets seem to fall dead.
His cry is like a lion’s;
His strength seems to have overflowed.
Unable to withstand his might,
Khans, common folk, and living creatures
Seem to flee in terrified haste.
Sarybai has ridden out for single combat—
Such is your monster.
He looks ready to slaughter his opponent,
To gnaw apart whoever meets him;
His baleful venom is so great
That he seems ready to swallow anyone he encounters.
Such is the hero’s ferocity.
His figure is like a mountain ridge,
His blue-black hardness is like iron.
When you behold his wrath and venom,
He seems ready to devour the living—
Such is his valor.
Brave Sarybai has come as a warrior;
From the infidel’s fury,
The black earth itself shook.
